source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Core model. A blend network has input spaces, a generic space (what the inputs share), a cross-space mapping of counterparts, and a blended space that gets selected structure from the inputs. The blend can hold structure that neither input has.
numbers: Four-space diagram built on the Buddhist monk riddle. No experiment, no sample. The expanded paper runs about 2300 lines of text.
quote: Conceptual integration--"blending"--is a general cognitive operation on a par with analogy, recursion, mental modeling, conceptual categorization, and framing.
limits: Built from hand-chosen cases. The authors say the data 'suggest' psychological experiments but they run none.
agent_relevance: Gives the named parts we would need to code an O7 / S3 blend step: two inputs, a typed mapping, a shared schema, a projection list, a blend.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Buddhist monk riddle. A monk goes up a mountain one day and down the next on the same path. Is there a spot he passes at the same time of day? Put the two days on one path and you get two walkers who must meet. The meeting spot answers the riddle for the original trip.
numbers: Counterparts: mountain, mover, day, motion. Generic space: a mover on a path on a day, with no direction or date. In the blend two days fuse into one day d' and the mover splits into two walkers.
limits: Intuitive demonstration only. No solve-rate data in this paper for people with or without the blend.
agent_relevance: A clean test case for a coded blend: the answer comes from running the blend (two walkers) and reading the result back onto the inputs. Good candidate for a unit test of a blend operator.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Three operations build emergent structure. Composition puts input elements together and creates relations that neither input has. Completion recruits background frames by pattern completion. Elaboration runs the blend as a mental simulation, and can go on indefinitely.
numbers: Monk: composition gives two travelers on one path; completion supplies the familiar 'two people walking toward each other' frame; elaboration yields the meeting.
limits: The paper does not say when to stop elaborating or how to tell a useful elaboration from drift.
agent_relevance: Maps to a stepwise operator: compose, complete (retrieve a frame), elaborate (run it). The 'run the blend' step needs a check by code (G3, G10), since the model's account of what the blend shows is not evidence.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Projection is selective. Not everything in the inputs goes into the blend. Calendar time of the monk trip is dropped. In the Kant debate, Kant's German, his death and his ignorance of the professor are dropped.
numbers: Monk: calendar date explicitly not projected. Kant debate: time, language, mode of expression, being dead, never knowing the professor are all left out.
limits: No rule is given for what to drop. Selection is left to optimality pressures that compete.
agent_relevance: The projection list is a place where code can enforce discipline: write down what is kept and what is dropped, so a later check can see what was assumed.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Debate with Kant. A philosopher says 'Kant disagrees with me... I answer...'. Neither input holds a debate. The blend places both in one room, one language, one topic. The debate frame is recruited by completion and supplies the vocabulary.
numbers: Counterparts: Kant and the professor, languages, topics, claims, times, goals, modes of expression. Authors say this blend is so conventional that it goes unnoticed.
limits: Shows blends are everyday, but the evidence is the authors' reading of one sentence.
agent_relevance: Shows how a frame (here debate) is imported to organize two non-interacting inputs. Could be a tag in the blend record: which frame was recruited and where it came from.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Regatta. A 1993 catamaran Great America II is compared to the 1853 clipper Northern Light on the same route. The blend is a live race. That gives the claim 'barely maintaining a 4.5 day lead' and an emotional value that flows back to the single-boat run.
numbers: Lead stated as 4.5 days. Authors list more than one valid reading of the blend (different time offsets, different courses), so the result is not unique.
limits: Blends are not deterministic. The same inputs support several blends, and the paper gives no way to pick one.
agent_relevance: Supports taking many independent blend attempts and selecting in code (G4, G5), not trusting one blend. Matches the S3 open-mode rule.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Optimality principles. Integration (the blend is a unit), Topology (relations match counterparts), Web (links to inputs kept without extra work), Unpacking (inputs can be rebuilt from the blend), Good reason (every element needs a role). Principles compete and give lower-level pressures such as non-disintegration and non-displacement.
numbers: Five principles named in section VI. Additional pressures listed (for example non-disintegration, non-displacement) for the computer desktop, regatta and Kant cases.
quote: Some blends are better than others.
limits: Principles are qualitative and not scored. The authors say some blends are better than others but give no scale.
agent_relevance: These five are a ready rubric for a coded blend check. Topology, Web and Unpacking can be tested by code (do mapped relations survive? can inputs be recovered?). Integration and Good reason need a run or a test, not a model opinion (G8).

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Authors say blending is not a compositional, algorithmic process and cannot be modeled as one for even rudimentary cases. A better analogy is biological evolution than chemical composition. They call computational modeling a formidable challenge.
numbers: No numbers. Stated in the introduction.
quote: Conceptual blending is not a compositional algorithmic process and cannot be modeled as such for even the most rudimentary cases.
limits: Strong claim by the theory's own authors. Later systems try a restricted version. The claim also makes the theory hard to test.
agent_relevance: Warns that a fixed rule-based blend operator will miss most blends. Fits a generate-many-then-select design (S3 plus code selection) better than a single deterministic procedure.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Compression and vital relations. Distant relations (time, space, cause, change, identity) in the network can be compressed into tight ones inside the blend. Elements that are not counterparts can still be combined in the blend through metonymic links. Example: the stork's diaper in the 'birth is arrival' blend.
numbers: Worked chain: 'change of state' + 'change of location' blends feed 'coming into existence', which feeds the Birth Stork blend. Also 'red-hot with anger' mixes heat, anger and body heat.
limits: Illustrative chain, no counts. Authors treat input spaces as often already being blends.
agent_relevance: Blends can be nested (output of one is input of another). A coded operator should allow a blend to be reused as an input, with its mapping kept.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Frame networks. When inputs share an organizing frame (monk, Kant, regatta), mapping is easy. Topology is split into TF (shared frame), TS (frame values that differ) and TI (incidental). Which features sit at which level can be promoted or demoted as the network is built.
numbers: Regatta example: clipper vs catamaran differ at TS level; dolphins and an uncharted island sit at TI level and become TS when they fill the 'obstacle' role.
limits: Descriptive taxonomy, not tested.
agent_relevance: Suggests the first step of a blend operator is to find the shared organizing frame. If none exists, mapping is hard and the blend is likely to be weak (links to the far-analogue variance note in O7).

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Authors claim evidence against all three claims in Gentner (1983) structure mapping: analogy is not compositional, mapping depends on content and not only on structure, and there are no clean kinds of projection, only gradients. Example: 'This surgeon is a butcher' means incompetence, which is in neither input.
numbers: Three counter-claims. The 'incompetence' meaning is the standard emergent-structure case.
limits: Argument by example. Structure-mapping researchers have disputed it, and the paper gives no controlled test.
agent_relevance: Warns that a pure structural mapping check (as in SME) misses emergent meaning. The blend needs a run or a test on the blend, not only a mapping score.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Blending as simulation tool. Hutchins (1995) reports a Micronesian navigator who solved a diagram problem by imagining himself sailing both directions between two islands at once, the monk structure in real life. The authors argue mental simulation of the scenario alone does not solve the monk riddle, but simulation of the blend does.
numbers: One reported navigator (Beiong), from Lewis (1972). Single anecdote.
limits: Anecdote, secondary report, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that the useful step is to simulate in the blended space and then project the result back to the inputs.

source: Fauconnier & Turner (1998) Conceptual Integration Networks (expanded web version 2001 of Cognitive Science 22(2):133-187)
finding: Authors list forerunners: Koestler (1964), Goffman (1974), Talmy (1977), Fong (1988), Moser and Hofstadter, Kunda, Miller and Clare (1990). They say these treated blends as exotic, and argue blends are central and pervasive.
numbers: Six forerunners named in the introduction.
limits: Kunda et al. (1990) is an experimental paper on combined social categories and is the only experimental forerunner in the list. Not opened here.
agent_relevance: The evidence base for blending in the founding paper is linguistic examples plus one psychology forerunner. Treat claims about general reasoning gain as untested.

source: Wikipedia: Bisociation (read 2026-11-01)
finding: Koestler defined bisociation as joining two or more apparently incompatible frames of thought ('matrices') into a new matrix of meaning, not mere association. Jokes work by a punch line that switches matrix. Scientific discovery fuses two matrices.
numbers: No numbers. Source is a short encyclopedia page about Koestler's The Act of Creation (1964).
limits: Secondary page. It does not equate bisociation with blending and gives no data.
agent_relevance: Forerunner for the S3 open-mode idea of joining two distant frames. The joke case shows an expected-then-switched structure which a coded step could imitate.

source: Wikipedia: Conceptual blending (read 2026-11-01)
finding: Summary of the field. The four-space network (generic, input, cross-space mapping, blend). Network types: simplex, mirror, single-scope, double-scope. Critics: Gibbs (2000) says no testable hypotheses and that process is inferred from products; Ritchie (2004) says it is more complex than needed. Computational lines: Shrager in the 1980s, Guhe et al. 2011 on mathematics, Lieto and Pozzato on description-logic concept combination.
numbers: Network types: 4. Named critics: 2 (Gibbs 2000, Ritchie 2004). Named computational lines: 3.
limits: Encyclopedia page, not primary. The fetch summary said nothing on Gentner or Murphy critiques.
agent_relevance: Tells us the main published objection is lack of testability. So our own blend operator must be judged by measured gain at equal tokens (G7), not by whether blends look insightful.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study. Memory & Cognition 30(6)
finding: ERP test of blending. Eighteen adults read sentences ending in a literal word, a 'literal mapping' word (literal sense but invites mapping across domains) or a metaphor word. N400 at 300-500 ms grew with integration demand: literal smallest, literal mapping middle, metaphor largest.
numbers: N=18 (14 men, 4 women, mean age 26). 165 sentence triplets. Metaphor vs literal N400: F(1,17)=6.86, p<.02. Main effect of sentence F(2,34)=3.90, p<.05. Literal mapping did not differ significantly from metaphor (F=2.03) or literal (F=2.18).
limits: Small sample. N400 reflects general semantic difficulty, so it does not isolate blending. The middle condition was not reliably different from either end.
agent_relevance: Weak human evidence that the cost of combining two domains rises in steps, not as a metaphor-versus-literal split. Little to say for an LLM agent beyond that integration has a cost.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study. Memory & Cognition 30(6)
finding: Gradient fit. A linear trend across the three conditions accounted for more than 98% of the N400 variance due to sentence type. A coding that put literal and literal mapping at the same level fit worse (about 40% of that variance). A later posterior positivity was largest for metaphors.
numbers: Linear trend: over 98% of condition variance. Alternative coding (1,1,3): about 40%. Mean metaphoricity ratings 1.4 (literal), 1.9 (literal mapping), 4.4 (metaphor); metaphor vs literal mapping F(1,17)=451.7, p<.0001. 55% of literal mapping items rated very literal vs 74% of literals.
quote: The results confirmed our central prediction of graded N400 amplitude across sentence-final words
limits: Ratings were collected after the ERP session from the same 18 people. The authors call the pattern consistent with blending, not proof of it.
agent_relevance: Supports treating the amount of blending as a gradient. For the schema this means a blend operator might be applied with a degree of mapping, not just on or off. Not a direct design rule.

source: Coulson & Van Petten (2002) Conceptual integration and metaphor: an event-related potential study. Memory & Cognition 30(6)
finding: Partial replication of Pynte, Besson, Robichon and Poli (1996), which used French familiar metaphors. The metaphor-versus-literal N400 gap reproduced in English. The new part was the middle condition. The N400 can also arise from comparison difficulty or low predictability, so other accounts fit.
numbers: Replication target: Pynte et al. 1996. Cloze procedure used to check the three sentence types. Data from 3 extra participants dropped (2 for eye artifacts, 1 for low test scores: PPVT-R 77, reading span 1.5).
limits: No ERP study separates blending from plain analogy or comparison.
agent_relevance: Shows the human data on blending are thin and not specific to blending.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models (CHI 23)
finding: PopBlends. A pipeline for blends between a pop-culture domain and a product. Stage 1 finds a connecting concept (three ways: no GPT, half GPT, full GPT-3). Stage 2 expands both sides into scenes tied to that concept and ranks scene pairs by semantic similarity.
numbers: Design: 5 pop-culture domains (Star Wars, Friends, Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, Breaking Bad) x 6 products (toothbrush, airplane, pizza, beer, cell phone, swimming). 15 connecting concepts per pair (5 per strategy).
limits: GPT-3 era model. Domain is advertising blends, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: A working example of a divergent step (expand each input) then a convergent step (match and rank by code). Same shape as the blend operator we have in mind.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models (CHI 23)
finding: Technical check of the connecting concepts. Over all three strategies 56.7% were rated relevant to both domains. Success rates were almost the same: no GPT 56.0%, half GPT 55.3%, full GPT 58.7%. At least one good concept in 5 tries: 93.3% of pairs (90.0%, 96.6%, 93.3% by strategy).
numbers: 10 annotators, two per domain. Cohen's kappa = .43 for stage 1 and .48 for stage 2 (moderate). A concept counted as good if either annotator said yes to both questions. Scene stage: 98.3% of pairs had at least one scene related to the concept.
limits: Lenient scoring (one yes is enough) and low agreement. Measures relevance only, not whether the blend is good or novel.
agent_relevance: Per-attempt success of about 56% with a 93% chance of at least one in five matches the 'many draws, then code selects' rule (G12 / S3). Keep the check by code, not by model opinion.

source: Wang, Petridis, Kwon, Ma, Chilton (2023) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models (CHI 23)
finding: User study. Ten amateur designers made pop-culture blends with PopBlends or a plain web-search baseline. They produced more than twice as many blend ideas with the tool and reported lower effort.
numbers: N=10, within subjects. Ideas per pair: 2.03 (SD 0.84) with PopBlends vs 0.87 (SD 0.56) baseline, Wilcoxon p<0.001. NASA-TLX: mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004), effort 3.05 vs 5.00 (p=0.006), performance 2.10 vs 3.60 (p=0.004), frustration 1.65 vs 3.25 (p=0.026). All 10 said PopBlends helped more.
limits: Tiny sample, student volunteers, baseline is web search, count of ideas not quality.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM-assisted structured blending raises the number of candidate ideas. It says nothing about idea quality, so under G8 the count alone does not justify the step.

source: Ge & Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models
finding: Visual blend pipeline. A language model finds a related object and writes a one-sentence blend description ('a moon sliced like an orange'). A text-to-image model then draws it. Language models beat ConceptNet at finding related concepts on a simile set, and larger models did better.
numbers: Precision on the simile dataset (Chakrabarty et al.): BERT-large P@10/100/1000 = 0.13/7.69/37.33; best model in the table 2.59/24.84/66.38; ConceptNet precision 'significantly lower'. 20 blend descriptions (half model-made, half by hand) used for the image study on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
limits: 2021 models (ELMo, BERT, GPT). P@1000 is a loose measure. Evaluation set of 20 is small. Image preferences are given only as a figure.
agent_relevance: Early result that associative retrieval for the mapping step is better done by a language model than by a hand-built knowledge base. Reasonable for the retrieval part of O7.

source: Olearo et al. (2025) Blending concepts with text-to-image diffusion models
finding: Four zero-shot ways to blend two prompts in a text-to-image diffusion model (textual embedding mix, UNet mix, alternate prompts, switch prompts). No method wins everywhere. Prompt order, conceptual distance and random seed change the result.
numbers: User study N=100 (age 19-25), 22 prompt pairs, 84 images, 5 categories, participants ranked four methods. Preference proportions: alternate over textual 0.60 (p<0.001), switch over textual 0.61, alternate over UNet 0.57, switch over UNet 0.58, UNet over textual 0.55 (all p<0.001); alternate vs switch 0.51 (p=0.31).
limits: Ranking by how coherent a blend looks, after a 10-minute intro to blending. Effect sizes small (55-61%). Images only; seed variability not tested in the study.
agent_relevance: Shows blend output is sensitive to input order and seed. Supports running both orders and several seeds in an open-mode blend, then selecting by code.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE), arXiv 2509.21043 v6
finding: KOMBINE benchmark of combinatorial creativity: association, analogy and blending between random entity pairs. The blend task asks for a generic space g and a blended concept with properties tagged from input u, from input v, shared (uv), or emergent. Blends are scored for utility, coherence and emergent structure by a three-LLM judge panel.
numbers: 35 LLMs, temperature 0.9, entities from Wikidata with at least 78 sitelinks. Judges: Claude Haiku 4.5, gpt-o3, GPT-5.4. Judge-human agreement 75% on items where all three judges agree (n=96), 66% when the majority agrees. Leaderboard on unanimous items correlates with the full one at Spearman 0.945 (n=21).
limits: Scoring is by LLM judges, and G5 and G8 say model judges are weak. Entities are random pairs, so many pairs have no good blend. A preprint at v6.
agent_relevance: The closest benchmark to a blend operator with the generic-space step made explicit. Its judge-agreement figures show an LLM-judged blend score is only moderately reliable.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE), arXiv 2509.21043 v6
finding: LLMs are worse at blends than at associations or analogies. Over 35 models a valid blend was found 43.4% of the time, a valid analogy 53.4% and a factual association 59.0%. The top model differs by task: claude-opus-4.6 led association and analogy, gpt-5.6-sol led blending at 64.8% valid blends (55.4% on analogy).
numbers: Averages over 35 models. Correlations between tasks: association-analogy r=0.71, analogy-blending r=0.70, blending-association r=0.54 (all p<0.001). Every entity pair got at least one valid blend from some model.
limits: Aggregate, not true of every model. Validity is by the judge panel.
agent_relevance: Even frontier models fail a large share of blends without any scaffold. A blend operator inside the schema must be checked before use, and may need a retry (S5).

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE), arXiv 2509.21043 v6
finding: Abstraction bottleneck. The hard part of a blend is finding a shared generic space. Models found a valid generic space only 43.4% of the time. Given a valid one, they described a coherent blended concept 97.1% of the time.
numbers: 43.4% (generic space valid), then 97.1% (coherent blend given a valid generic space). Example failure: a generic space that applies only to bread for (Photosynthesis, Bread).
limits: The authors guess at a cause (lack of experiential knowledge) without testing it. The 97.1% is conditional on passing the first check.
agent_relevance: Key design pointer: put the checking effort on the generic-space step, which a coded checker can test (does it fit both inputs?). Blend elaboration is not where models fail.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE), arXiv 2509.21043 v6
finding: Inventive homogeneity. Different LLMs invent the same concepts. Blends are far more likely than analogies to repeat another model's properties, and models from one provider are more alike.
numbers: 2,070 concepts, 7,868 properties; 19.9% (412/2,070) are multiples at k=2 (cosine threshold 0.674, 99th percentile). Blends vs analogies: 94.7% vs 36.3% at k=1; 37.3% vs 2.6% at k=2 (14.3x). Same provider 9.3% vs different provider 4.1% (2.3x). DeepSeek +12.2 pp, Anthropic +11.1 pp above baseline, OpenAI -1.4 pp.
limits: Embedding similarity of property text decides what counts as a multiple. The blend prompt was one fixed template asking for one blend, which may push all models toward the same schema.
agent_relevance: Supports G4 (samples from one model are not independent) and the S3 open-mode rule of tracking directions tried. Several blends from one model or family will repeat each other.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE), arXiv 2509.21043 v6
finding: Humans vs LLMs. 75 people scored below nearly every LLM on all three tasks, mostly because they found fewer valid connections. Both found blending hardest. Humans find analogy easier than association; LLMs the other way around. The two groups use different regions of semantic space.
numbers: N=75 after screening 120 Prolific adults (mean age 40.1). 5 items per task. Valid rates humans vs LLMs: association 22.1% vs 59.0%, analogy 32.9% vs 53.4%, blending 12.8% vs 43.4%. Skipped items scored zero.
limits: Online crowd workers with short time, no expert group. Zero for skipped items pushes the human numbers down.
agent_relevance: Gives a human baseline of 12.8% valid blends, so LLM blend skill is not low in absolute terms, but humans and models cover different ground. Hints at value in adding retrieved human-made analogues (S3).

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE), arXiv 2509.21043 v6
finding: Background note from KOMBINE: no large-scale conceptual blending benchmark for LLMs existed before it. Song et al. (2025) found LLMs struggle to make noun phrases with emergent properties (for example 'peeled apple' gains 'white'). Wang et al. 2023 (PopBlends) is the small-scale prior.
numbers: No new numbers. Statement is the paper's own literature review.
limits: Song et al. 2025 was not opened; the claim is relayed from KOMBINE.
agent_relevance: Confirms that measured LLM blending evidence is thin before 2025 and that the emergent-property step is the weak point.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics, and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs
finding: A short review that treats prompts as blends and defines Prompt-Induced Transitions and Prompt-Induced Hallucinations. It argues that blending semantically distant prompts causes shifts in tone or invented content. It proposes prompt engineering as a way to probe how meaning is compressed.
numbers: No new measured results found in the text read. Cites the author's earlier arXiv work (2505.00557) for quantitative claims.
limits: Conceptual essay with little data. A web-search summary of it claimed a human-vs-LLM fusion difference; I could not find that in the text.
agent_relevance: Weak source. Do not use it as evidence that LLMs blend like people. One useful reminder: blends of distant inputs can cause confident but invented content, so check the blend against the inputs.

source: Bing & Redish (2006/2007) The cognitive blending of mathematics and physics knowledge
finding: Applied blending to physics students working with math. Single-scope blends take the frame of one input (math machinery) and import few elements from the other. Double-scope blends integrate both frames. Projecting a blend result back to the physical input exposed an error: an answer of 47,500 seconds was unreasonable.
numbers: Qualitative video cases of physics majors (air drag and a car problem). Answer 47,500 seconds for a 500 ft trip. The same student answered correctly (2 seconds) once simple numbers activated the physical input.
limits: Few cases, no counts or rates. Authors say blending is nonlinear and nondeterministic and that their reading is one reasonable reading.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the step 'project the blend result back to the inputs and check it'. A reasonableness test against the other input caught the error.

source: Bing & Redish (2006/2007) The cognitive blending of mathematics and physics knowledge
finding: Blend topology has inertia. Students who start with a heavily single-scope blend tend to stay in it. A move to a double-scope blend usually needs a strong perturbation, for instance new evidence or a question that activates the neglected input.
numbers: Qualitative observation across the cases analysed. No frequencies given.
limits: Observation by the researchers; no coding scheme or inter-rater check reported in the 4-page paper.
agent_relevance: A blend dominated by one input needs a deliberate push (a check or a question tied to the other input) to be corrected. Fits the idea that a failed check should drive the next step (G2).

source: Dreyfus, Gupta, Redish (2014) Applying conceptual blending to model coordinated use of multiple ontological metaphors
finding: Education case study: a physics professor and an undergraduate both blend two metaphors for energy (a substance and a vertical location) into one mental model, shown through speech and gesture analysis.
numbers: Data: classroom recordings of one professor, and an interview with one undergraduate (pseudonym Betsy). Predicate analysis plus gesture analysis; no counts.
limits: Two cases. Authors say their analysis does not address the misconception debate (Chi and Slotta).
agent_relevance: Shows blending used as a descriptive tool. Evidence that experts coordinate two models at once, but not evidence that doing so improves answers.
